lecture.New_Day13Part1audio01.mp3: Welcome to Day 13! Today we master one of the most transformative concepts in relational database analytics: Subqueries. A subquery allows you to embed one query inside another, unlocking multi-step filtering, benchmarks, and advanced row-by-row comparisons.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio02.mp3: What is a subquery? Simply put, it is an inner SELECT statement enclosed in parentheses. The database executes the subquery first, or row-by-row, and passes its result directly to the outer query.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio03.mp3: Subqueries are classified into four primary types: Scalar subqueries, Multi-row subqueries, Derived Tables in the FROM clause, and Correlated subqueries.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio04.mp3: A Scalar subquery returns exactly one row and one column — a single atomic value. Because it evaluates to a solitary value, you can place it anywhere a constant or column name is valid.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio05.mp3: In Query 1, we filter for employees earning more than the company average. The inner query computes the average salary once, and the outer WHERE clause filters against that numeric benchmark.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio06.mp3: You can also place scalar subqueries directly in the SELECT list. Here, we calculate each employee's salary variance from the company-wide average in a single readable statement.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio07.mp3: When an inner query produces multiple values, it is a Multi-Row subquery. We compare against this list using operators like in, not in, ANY, or ALL.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio08.mp3: In Query 2, we return customers whose customer ID appears in the list of distinct customer IDs from the orders table.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio09.mp3: A subquery placed in the FROM clause is called a Derived Table or Inline View. It creates a temporary virtual table that exists only for that query, and standard SQL requires you to assign it an alias.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio10.mp3: In Query 3, we calculate the average of departmental average salaries. This requires two tiers of aggregation that cannot be solved in a standard flat SELECT statement.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio11.mp3: A Correlated subquery is special: it references a column from the outer table. The inner query cannot run independently — the database re-executes it once for every candidate row in the outer query.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio12.mp3: In Query 4, we find employees who earn more than the average salary of their own specific department by correlating on department ID.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio13.mp3: The EXISTS and NOT EXISTS operators test whether an inner subquery returns at least one matching row. They return a boolean true or false and short-circuit immediately on the first found record.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio14.mp3: In Query 5, we use NOT EXISTS to pinpoint customers who have never placed an order. This provides superior performance and NULL safety compared to legacy techniques.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio15.mp3: Beware the dangerous NOT in with NULL trap! If a subquery returns even a single NULL value, NOT in evaluates to UNKNOWN for every single row, causing your query to return zero results. Always prefer NOT EXISTS.
lecture.New_Day13Part1audio16.mp3: You now possess the foundational theory of SQL subqueries! Let's head over to the editor and solve 15 production analytics challenges.

questions.New_Day13Question01.mp3: Above average earners! From employees, return first name, last name, and salary for all employees earning more than the company average salary.
questions.New_Day13Question01sol.mp3: Let's filter with a scalar subquery. SELECT first name, last name, salary FROM employees WHERE salary > in parentheses SELECT AVG of salary FROM employees.
questions.New_Day13Question02.mp3: Salary variance from average! Return first name, salary, and variance calculated as salary minus company average salary from employees, ordered by variance descending.
questions.New_Day13Question02sol.mp3: Let's compute variance in SELECT. SELECT first name, salary, salary - in parentheses SELECT AVG of salary FROM employees as variance FROM employees ORDER BY variance DESC.
questions.New_Day13Question03.mp3: Purchasing customers! Return customer ID, first name, and email for customers whose customer ID is in the orders table.
questions.New_Day13Question03sol.mp3: Let's use a multi-row IN subquery. SELECT customer ID, first name, email FROM customers WHERE customer ID IN in parentheses SELECT DISTINCT customer ID FROM orders.
questions.New_Day13Question04.mp3: Products in fulfilled orders! Return name and unit price for products whose product ID is in order items where the parent order status is Shipped.
questions.New_Day13Question04sol.mp3: Let's check product IDs with IN. SELECT name, unit price FROM products WHERE product ID IN in parentheses SELECT oi.product ID FROM order items oi JOIN orders o ON oi.order ID = o.order ID WHERE o.status = Shipped.
questions.New_Day13Question05.mp3: Find non-purchasing customers! Return customer ID and first name for customers who have no record in the orders table using NOT IN, ensuring order customer ID is not null.
questions.New_Day13Question05sol.mp3: Let's filter with NOT IN. SELECT customer ID, first name FROM customers WHERE customer ID NOT IN in parentheses SELECT customer ID FROM orders WHERE customer ID IS NOT NULL.
questions.New_Day13Question06.mp3: Highest earner per department! From employees, return first name, salary, department ID, and dept max salary using a correlated subquery in the SELECT clause.
questions.New_Day13Question06sol.mp3: Let's correlate in SELECT. SELECT e1.first name, e1.salary, e1.department ID, in parentheses SELECT MAX of e2.salary FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.department ID = e1.department ID as dept max salary FROM employees e1.
questions.New_Day13Question07.mp3: Above departmental average! Return first name, salary, and department ID for employees who earn more than the average salary of their own department.
questions.New_Day13Question07sol.mp3: Let's correlate in WHERE. SELECT first name, salary, department ID FROM employees e1 WHERE salary > in parentheses SELECT AVG of salary FROM employees e2 WHERE e2.department ID = e1.department ID.
questions.New_Day13Question08.mp3: Average of department payrolls! Using a derived table in FROM, calculate the average of total department payrolls as avg dept payroll.
questions.New_Day13Question08sol.mp3: Let's aggregate from a derived table. SELECT AVG of dept payroll as avg dept payroll FROM in parentheses SELECT department ID, SUM of salary as dept payroll FROM employees GROUP BY department ID as summaries.
questions.New_Day13Question09.mp3: Crown highest paid employee! Return first name, job title, and salary for the employee who earns the maximum salary across the entire company.
questions.New_Day13Question09sol.mp3: Let's find the max earner. SELECT first name, job title, salary FROM employees WHERE salary = in parentheses SELECT MAX of salary FROM employees.
questions.New_Day13Question10.mp3: Verify active buyers with EXISTS! Return customer ID and first name for customers where an order exists in orders.
questions.New_Day13Question10sol.mp3: Let's test with EXISTS. SELECT customer ID, first name FROM customers c WHERE EXISTS in parentheses SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer ID = c.customer ID.
questions.New_Day13Question11.mp3: Audit inactive accounts with NOT EXISTS! Return customer ID and first name for customers who have zero records in orders using NOT EXISTS.
questions.New_Day13Question11sol.mp3: Let's test with NOT EXISTS. SELECT customer ID, first name FROM customers c WHERE NOT EXISTS in parentheses SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer ID = c.customer ID.
questions.New_Day13Question12.mp3: Products priced above category average! Return name, category ID, and unit price for products with unit price greater than the average unit price in their category.
questions.New_Day13Question12sol.mp3: Let's compare category averages. SELECT name, category ID, unit price FROM products p1 WHERE unit price > in parentheses SELECT AVG of unit price FROM products p2 WHERE p2.category ID = p1.category ID.
questions.New_Day13Question13.mp3: Departments with high headcount! Return department name from departments where department ID is in departments with more than 2 employees.
questions.New_Day13Question13sol.mp3: Let's filter departments with IN. SELECT department name FROM departments WHERE department ID IN in parentheses SELECT department ID FROM employees GROUP BY department ID HAVING COUNT star > 2.
questions.New_Day13Question14.mp3: High-volume spenders via derived table! Query a derived table of customer order totals to return customer ID and total spent for customers who spent 50000 or more.
questions.New_Day13Question14sol.mp3: Let's filter derived spenders. SELECT customer ID, total spent FROM in parentheses SELECT customer ID, SUM of total amount as total spent FROM orders GROUP BY customer ID as spenders WHERE total spent >= 50000.
questions.New_Day13Question15.mp3: Orders with above-average item quantities! Return distinct order ID from order items where qty is greater than the overall average item quantity.
questions.New_Day13Question15sol.mp3: Let's filter order items. SELECT DISTINCT order ID FROM order items WHERE qty > in parentheses SELECT AVG of qty FROM order items.
